newsitem.title: KENYA: Kenya braces for national strike, fears violence.
newsitem.headline: Kenya braces for national strike, fears violence.

text.p: Kenya braced for a national strike on Friday called by opposition groups demanding pre-election political reforms from President Daniel arap Moi.
The level of backing for the protest will be an acid test both for the divided opposition and for a government weakened by a run on the currency, labour unrest and corruption scandals.
The capital Nairobi was tense ahead of the planned strike which Labour Minister Philip Masinde declared unlawful.

Most city centre shops and many offices were expected to be closed for the day with people fearing a repeat of the violence and looting which usually mars political protests in the East African country.
"Most people will stay at home because they are frightened for their safety, not because they support the strike," one Nairobi lawyer predicted.
The feared General Service Unit (GSU), Kenya's paramilitary anti-riot force, stepped up patrols on Thursday.

The political climate has degenerated steadily in the past two months and at least nine people were killed on July 7 in clashes between police and pro-reform demonstrators in Nairobi and other centres.
The cause of the tension is the presidential and parliamentary election which must be held this year but whose date Moi has yet to announce.

The 73-year-old leader, in power since 1978, wants a final five-year term. A few weeks ago western diplomats said he looked almost unbeatable against an opposition divided by tribe and personal ambition and handicapped by pro-regime laws.
"But in the last few days Moi seems to have lost his sureness of touch," a senior diplomat commented on Thursday.
The jittery mood was reflected in the fortunes of the shilling currency, one of the most solid in Africa since 1994.
It sank to an historic low on Thursday, closing at a commercial average of 70.26 to the dollar despite Central Bank intervention.
The shilling has lost more than 18 percent since the International Monetary Fund (IMF) halted a $205 million aid package a week ago, citing the government's failure to crack down on corruption.
In Washington the IMF gave a cool reception on Thursday to apparent peace overtures from Finance Minister Musalia Mudavadi who said Kenya was ready to talk about the terms of a new loan.
An IMF spokesman said Kenya first had to take "fundamental measures to address governance issues".
Moi won some respite when air traffic controllers agreed to suspend a five-day go-slow which brought chaos to passenger and cargo flights.
Organisers of the national strike have scheduled protest rallies on Friday in Nairobi's central Uhuru park and in 11 provincial towns in the country of nearly 30 million people.

The pressure is equally on the opposition to show it can mobilise large numbers of supporters at demonstrations. The turn-out in previous protests has been modest, depending heavily on students, unemployed youths and abandoned street children living rough.
Even before it happened the strike provided more evidence of opposition divisions with two leaders, Kenneth Matiba and Kijana Wamalwa, refusing to support it.
Some in the opposition prefer dialogue following Moi's assent to limited political reforms before the polls and a full constitutional review afterwards.
Others reject any compromise saying Moi's ruling Kenya African National Union (KANU) and civil servants will rig the elections unless there is a prior clean-up.
